children: Wild swings among individual stocks are renewing hedge fund interest in dispersion trades as investors try to capitalize on sharply different winners and losers from artificial intelligence, higher interest rates and geopolitical turmoil, Bloomberg News reported Sunday.

Enthusiasm over advances in agentic AI has collided with concerns that the technology could disrupt industries ranging from banking to travel. At the same time, developments in the Iran and Ukraine wars have driven sharp moves in energy stocks, while Treasury yields at two-decade highs have increased borrowing costs.

The result is a market in which individual stocks can move dramatically even when major indexes remain relatively subdued. That environment can favor dispersion strategies, which generally seek to profit when volatility among individual stocks exceeds volatility in a broader index such as the S&P 500 (

Rising dispersion suggests the market is becoming less driven by broad themes and more by company-specific risks and opportunities. That could increase the importance of stock selection during earnings season, particularly among companies exposed to AI disruption, energy prices and higher borrowing costs. It could also create opportunities for options traders betting on larger moves in individual shares than in the overall market.

Single-stock implied volatility has fallen since late July, particularly among technology companies, making options on some individual stocks cheaper than they were earlier in the summer. At the same time, traders have begun buying more single-stock options while selling volatility on indexes.
Nomura strategist Charlie McElligott said the one-month absolute returns of individual S&P 500 (

) stocks relative to the index recently reached the 95th percentile of observations over the past 30 years. Measures of correlation among stocks have also declined again after recovering from unusually low levels in July.
AI widens the gap between winners and losers

Technology offers some of the clearest examples. Investors are reassessing which software companies could benefit from AI and which face disruption, producing large differences in share-price performance.
Energy offers another potential dispersion opportunity. Oil producers and refiners can respond differently to changes in crude prices, geopolitical developments and refining margins.
The approaching earnings season could amplify those differences as investors focus more closely on company-specific results and outlooks.

Still, dispersion has become a popular hedge fund strategy in recent years, raising concerns that the trade may be crowded. Kris Sidial, co-chief investment officer at Ambrus Group, cautioned that its popularity could leave the strategy vulnerable to a reversal.

Other investors are taking simpler approaches. Alon Rosin, head of institutional equity derivatives at Oppenheimer, said investors can concentrate on a smaller group of stocks while using puts on broad ETFs such as the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust
Demand for options remains strong. Average options volume increased 14% in August from a year earlier, according to Options Clearing Corp. data.

AI remains the largest source of uncertainty. Its effects could extend well beyond technology into power generation, real estate, retail and employment. That leaves investors confronting unusually wide potential outcomes for companies most exposed to the technology.

For dispersion traders, that uncertainty is precisely the attraction: the bigger the divide between AI's eventual winners and losers, the greater the potential difference between individual-stock volatility and movements in the broader market, Bloomberg News reported.

title: AI-driven stock swings revive hedge fund interest in dispersion trades
